text: Testing and proof answer different questions. A test is existential: it hunts for a witness that something breaks, and a run that finds nothing tells you this artifact has no defect of the kinds your method can see, in the regions you looked. A proof is universal: it establishes that every execution, over an unbounded input space, satisfies a property, so it rules out the existence of any such witness. Both are complete only with respect to a chosen class of defect, and both become dishonest the moment you forget which class you chose.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: In Lean a proof is a program. Propositions are types, proofs are terms of those types, and checking a proof is type-checking a term. That is the Curry-Howard correspondence, and it is literally how the implementation works. It is also why the tactic language can be arbitrarily clever or arbitrarily buggy at no cost to soundness: whatever a tactic emits still has to satisfy a kernel of a few thousand lines. The induction tactic, for instance, is a macro that emits a call to Nat.recAux, and what survives is a lambda term.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: The specification is where formal verification goes wrong, and it goes wrong quietly. Take a withdraw function over Nat, the type every ERC-20 reaches for as uint256. A theorem saying the balance never goes negative is provable and says nothing at all, because Nat subtraction truncates at zero and 0 <= x holds of every Nat that has ever existed. The theorem quantified over nothing, the auditor got a checkmark, and tokens can still evaporate.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: The property that carries information about withdraw is conservation, and Lean rejects it because it is false. The rejection is the useful part: the error names the failure region directly, reporting that a possible counterexample may satisfy amt - bal >= 1. Adding the precondition h : amt <= bal makes the theorem go through. That hypothesis is the require() nobody wrote, and the spec is what found it.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Truncating and wrapping arithmetic is a real class of bug rather than a teaching toy. Years of integer underflow drains, where a balance of 5 minus 100 wrapped to a number near 2^256, are why Solidity 0.8 made overflow checks the default in 2020. Lean's Nat clamps to zero instead of wrapping, so the failure is quieter, and the shape is identical: an arithmetic type whose edge behavior nobody wrote a spec about.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Vacuity is the one bad-spec failure mode you can hunt mechanically. If a theorem's hypotheses contradict each other then everything follows and the kernel will certify all of it, so withdraw_pays_you and withdraw_pays_you_differently can both be green with conclusions that cannot both hold. The check almost nobody runs is whether any input satisfies the preconditions at all, which is itself a machine-checkable statement. Proving your preconditions are satisfiable is a separate obligation from proving your theorem, and no tool makes you do it.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Generating candidate invariants with a language model moves the spec bottleneck without removing it. Knowing what to prove used to be expensive because the only source of candidate properties was somebody who had already seen that class of bug, and a model that has read a lot of code proposes hundreds of candidates cheaply while the prover kills the false ones deterministically. The generator is allowed to be wrong; the checker is the half that has to be right. What the loop does not touch is vacuity. A generated candidate can be a statement nothing could violate, exactly the way a human one can, and the loop's reward signal is that the prover said yes, which is maximized by proposing trivially true properties. Checking that the preconditions are satisfiable at all therefore becomes the filter such a loop needs rather than a curiosity.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: The assurance ladder for software correctness runs unit tests, then fuzzing, then an audit, then formal verification, each rung more burdensome in human hours than the one below it. Most teams historically stopped at the second rung because of what the fourth cost. Agents cheapened every rung at the same time, so the distance between the cheap rungs and the expensive one closed, and the question of why a team would stop below the rung that quantifies over every execution got harder to answer. There is no published benchmark for what fraction of machine-generated invariants survive contact with a prover, so claims of this shape should be asked for a number.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: A verified compiler is three artifacts: a formal semantics of the source language, a formal semantics of the target, and a semantic preservation theorem tying them together. CompCert's version says informally that for any source program that does not go wrong, any behavior the compiled program produces is a behavior the source was allowed to produce. The hedges carry the weight. It is refinement rather than equality, which is what makes optimization legal at all; "does not go wrong" excludes undefined behavior, so a UB program gets no guarantee; and it covers observable behavior only, so a verified compiler can still introduce a timing side-channel.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Emitting the cheaper subtree first is a genuine optimizer move, and on a small expression compiler it is correct for plus and times because those commute, so the proof closes those cases through Nat.add_comm and Nat.mul_comm. It fails on exactly one constructor out of five. Lean localizes the bug to that single case and prints the false equation the optimization would need, eval env b - eval env a = eval env a - eval env b. A test suite written by someone who mostly exercises addition would have shipped it.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Finding the right induction hypothesis is most of the work in every real verification project, CompCert included. The statement you want about compiling an expression concerns an empty stack, and that statement is unprovable by induction, because compiling plus a b runs compile b on a stack that already holds a's result. So you prove the stronger claim about every stack and recover the weaker one you asked for as a one-liner. The other trick is negative: eval and run must share no code, since defining the machine by calling the evaluator would make the theorem true, checked, and vacuous.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Two different machines are both called formal verification and they share almost nothing except the name. Interactive theorem proving, which is what Lean does, has the human supply a proof term that the kernel type-checks; it reaches unbounded structures and arbitrary mathematics, and it costs months of work. The other machine never builds a proof term at all: it walks the program symbolically so that each instruction becomes a constraint over symbolic inputs rather than an operation on values, then hands the resulting constraint system to an SMT solver such as Z3 and asks whether any assignment violates the property. Nobody writes a proof, and a failure returns a concrete counterexample input. The price is that the solver gives up: a state space it cannot bound returns unknown, which is the usual answer on anything with an unbounded loop.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Automated verification of smart contracts runs on bytecode rather than on source, and the reason is the verified-compiler argument arriving from the other direction. What executes is bytecode, so any higher level reasoned over instead is a model of it, and a model fails two ways: the compiler that produced the bytes can be wrong, and the model drifts when somebody edits the source and nobody re-derives it. Proving over the bytes closes both gaps, at the cost of reasoning in a language with no types, names or structure, which is why that side has to be automated. The same reasoning explains why the practice found its first routine commercial home on blockchains: symbolic execution dies on unbounded computation and every EVM execution is bounded because it pays gas per step, contracts are thousands of lines where a browser is millions, and the cost of being wrong is the balance sitting in the contract. Bounded, small, and expensive to get wrong is a rare combination.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: On 28 July 2026 a claimed proof of the Collatz conjecture in under 300 lines passed Lean's official kernel and also passed nanoda, an independent checker written from scratch in about 5,000 lines of Rust. It was hitting two separate bugs, one in each. In Lean's case, eliminating a nested occurrence of an inductive type dropped the parametric arguments from the generated auxiliary types, which escaped type checking and produced an axiom-free proof of False. The fix merged at 13:39 UTC that day and Lean v4.32.2 published at 16:34 UTC, just under three hours later.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: #print axioms is the sanity check people reach for, and its reach is narrower than its reputation. It catches sorry, and it catches native_decide, which compiles to machine code and trusts the result, where the system correctly tells on itself. It cannot see a bad specification: the vacuously-true withdraw theorem reports an axiom list as innocent as propext and Quot.sound, which appear throughout Mathlib. In the Collatz case the report read that the proof of False depends on no axioms at all. The command audits the logical dependencies of a valid derivation, so a kernel that accepted an invalid one is invisible to it.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: The defense against kernel soundness bugs is diversity rather than a single better kernel. nanoda, lean4checker and Lean4Lean are independently implemented, so an exploit has to beat all of them at once, and the Collatz proof was news precisely because it beat two. The pressure is now structural: a prover trained by reinforcement learning against a verifier will find whatever maximizes reward, and a soundness hole is the global maximum, which turns adversarial pressure on proof kernels from a PhD-scale activity into a machine-scale one.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Lawrence Paulson argued on 30 July 2026 that this is the predictable cost of Lean's design. Inductive types, pattern matching and recursion live inside Lean's kernel, whereas Isabelle's LCF architecture derives all of it from a tiny axiom set so the kernel stays minimal and such bugs have nowhere to live. His word for building those constructs into the kernel is theft. Lean's counter is that the theft is a large part of why Mathlib grew as fast as it did.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: OpenAI's ten proofs of open problems, published 1 August 2026, settle one thing cleanly: no step got hand-waved. Ten modules, 548,205 lines of Lean, 16,186 lines that open a theorem or a lemma, and a machine-readable manifest publishing sorry_count 0 per result. That had been the failure mode of every previous AI proof announcement. What it leaves standing is everything about specifications, because a kernel certificate says the derivation is valid and says nothing about whether the statement means what a reader thinks it means.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: The ten-proofs repository makes the human-facing split structural. Twelve ComparatorChallenges files carry the theorem statements and nothing else, every theorem stubbed with sorry, and a config points the Comparator tool at the module obliged to discharge them. Three details in that config are the whole argument: sorry has flipped sides and become the honest use, a file that states an obligation and pointedly refuses to discharge it; permitted_axioms promotes #print axioms to a release gate, whitelisting propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice across all twelve configs; and enable_nanoda switches on kernel diversity by default.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: The non-sofic group result is 39 lines of statement sitting on 34,440 lines addressed to the kernel, and reading the short file is where the difficulty moves. Four of those 39 lines are the theorem. The other thirty-five decide what Sofic means, building the word from normalizedHamming up through PermutationModel and an approximation condition. Put the wrong inequality in that definition and you get a green, kernel-checked, axiom-clean theorem about a notion that is not soficity, and nothing downstream will ever mention it. Across the twelve files it is 38 checked theorems resting on 195 definitions and 25 structures and classes, all of it upstream of anything a kernel can see.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: One detail from the ten-proofs repository is worth reading as a fact about the pinned checking stack rather than about the results. lean-toolchain pins v4.32.0, released 13 July 2026, and lakefile.toml pins mathlib and Comparator to the same tag. The kernel soundness fix shipped in v4.32.2 on 28 July, and its release note says the bug reached the standard kernel even when using the comparator tool, while separately advising an upgrade of nanoda for a bug of its own. The repository went public on 1 August. Triggering the bug takes a malicious meta program, nothing here suggests anyone wrote one, and the remedy is a one-line toolchain bump plus a rebuild.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: zkSecurity formalized a soundness proof for FRI in Lean, taking the round-by-round argument of Albert Garreta, Nicolas Mohnblatt and Benedikt Wagner over the protocol underneath most STARK-shaped proving systems in production. It took roughly a month and a half and was written with Harmonic's Aristotle and Claude Code rather than by hand, which is a current price for machine-checking one existing paper whose result nobody disputed. The delta is the part worth reading first: one result cited from the WHIR paper, on mutually correlated agreement, is left unformalized, and the formalization carries a condition the paper omits, that the initial degree is bigger than zero. Both are disclosed in the write-up. Their stated reason for the exercise is that the correctness of the proofs stops being dependent on somebody's rigor.
title: aadhar.sh: lean

text: Paradigm's two Solidity verification artifacts publish their own scope, which is the property that makes them trustworthy. SolidCore, the Lean 4 Solidity semantics, claims byte-identical observable behavior against solc 0.8.35 and claims it for single-contract programs with one entrypoint call, leaving external calls, contract creation, inline assembly and gas introspection outside the fence, with known divergences tracked in a log and a spec-hunt bounty paying for new ones. Solidus is earlier than its name suggests: the verified half is the Yul-to-EVM backend under a single compile_correct theorem, and the Solidity-to-Yul frontend does not exist yet, so the pipeline consumes optimized Yul from a pinned solc. Read those fences the way CompCert's hedges are read.
title: aadhar.sh: lean
